subject: Cert chain provenance and internal FQDN routing for Acme private deployment
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Elena Torres <security@acme.com>, platform@acme.com
Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.com, grace_oconnor@redwood.com, jonas_weber@redwood.com
Date: 2025-03-01T09:15:00-07:00
Subject: Cert chain provenance and internal FQDN routing for Acme private deployment

Hi Elena / Acme Platform team,

Thanks again for the walk-through yesterday. To make the handoff to our infra team smooth, I put together a short list of open questions and an initial assignable matrix (attached) about certificate provenance, routing of internal FQDNs, and termination points in the private deployment.

Top items we need clarity on from your side: 
- Root/trust model: do you require keys to be generated and kept in your HSM (customer-owned root) or would you accept a cross-signed intermediate that you own?
- FQDN ownership: which subdomains will Acme manage via split DNS? (e.g., private.acme.com vs. *.redwood-acme.internal)
- Termination: preferred TLS termination point — customer-facing edge (their proxy), Redwood private endpoint, or a mutual TLS proxy in the VPC?
- OCSP/CRL: any specific stapling/OCSP responder requirements and retention window for revocation artifacts?
- Rotation cadence and automation: can Acme accept short-lived certs (90 days) via ACME if keys are in an HSM, or do you need longer-lived certs with manual rotation?

What we propose from Redwood:
- Support for either customer-managed root (we will not ship private keys) or a cross-signed intermediate that you control via a CSR workflow.
- Option A (recommended): Customer owns DNS for private FQDNs (split-horizon) and we publish the internal A records to your VPC resolver. This minimizes trust surface and lets you rotate certs independently.
- Option B: Redwood issues certs for internal FQDNs using a customer-owned intermediate; Redwood runs an ACME client that stores certs encrypted and keys are wrapped by their KMS (customer key-wrapping).
- For mutual TLS, we can require client certs issued by your CA for inbound connections to Redwood endpoints.

Please see the attached cert-provenance-matrix.csv for a mapping between FQDNs, who owns the DNS record, who signs the cert, and the expected rotation cadence.

Next steps: if you can confirm the trust model and FQDN ownership by Monday, we'll draft an ops playbook (CSR exchange, ACME configuration, NGINX/TCP proxy mapping) and schedule a short handoff call with infra (Karthik, Jonas, Grace).

Best,

-- 
Marissa Cole
Head of Partnerships (acting)
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Cert chain provenance and internal FQDN routing for Acme private deployment

Marissa / Elena,

Quick technical notes from infra before the call: 

1) Root / intermediate pattern: if Acme can provide an intermediate signed by their root, that's ideal. We can accept an intermediate with the private key kept by Acme (mutual TLS pairing) or Acme can provide a cross-signed intermediate + CSR flow. If keys must never leave Acme HSM, we'll rely on TLS termination upstream (Acme proxy) or mTLS to the Redwood edge.

2) ACME feasibility: ACME is possible even with HSM-stored keys if you have an ACME client that supports external key stores (e.g., certbot with PKCS11). If that's not feasible, short-lived certs can still be automated via an agreed CSR rotation job (we'll run an orchestration hook in your VPC).

3) FQDN routing / split DNS: prefer that Acme own the private zones in their VPC resolver (Route53-private, Cloud DNS peering, on-prem BIND). We'll configure the Redwood side to only resolve via that resolver — avoids split-brain. For fallback, we can publish a shadow zone but that increases ops complexity.

4) Termination options: 
   - Terminate at Acme edge: simplest for their PKI constraints, but Redwood loses ability to inspect tokens for caching/optimizations.
   - Terminate at Redwood private endpoint: gives us full runtime control; requires acceptance of our cert model or a mutual TLS arrangement that accepts client certs from Acme.
   - mTLS proxy inside VPC: a lightweight TCP proxy with mTLS to both sides (Acme <-> proxy <-> Redwood) — trades latency for separation.

5) OCSP/CRL: we can optionally mirror CRL/OCSP responses into our internal cache for availability, but we need the responder URLs and expected TTL.

Attaching a short checklist to drive the call. Happy to sketch sample NGINX/Envoy config fragments if helpful.

-karthik

Subject: Re: Cert chain provenance and internal FQDN routing for Acme private deployment

Marissa / Karthik,

Thanks for the detailed questions and options. A few constraints from Acme's security/Product compliance team: 

- We cannot accept certs for internal FQDNs that are signed only by Redwood-managed roots. All certs presented to our clients must chain to Acme's enterprise root.
- Private key material for any server cert that represents an Acme FQDN must be generated and kept in our HSM. We can provide an intermediate signed by our root and will accept a CSR flow.
- For inbound connections to Redwood endpoints that will serve Acme traffic, we require mutual TLS: Redwood must present a cert signed by Acme's intermediate, and Redwood must validate client certs issued by Acme.
- OCSP: we run an internal OCSP responder. We need Redwood to support stapling and to present proof of stapling behavior in the first week of production.
- Rotation: minimum 180-day certs are acceptable, but our PKI team prefers automation so monthly rotation is ideal. We'll work with you on acceptable automation models; we can run an ACME endpoint internally that your automation can call if needed.

Attached is our acme-pki-requirements.pdf with specifics on CSR formats, accepted ciphers, and HSM vendor integrations.

Given the constraints, our preference is: Acme-managed intermediate (we sign), keys in Acme HSM, split DNS with Acme owning the private zones, and a mutual TLS termination at a lightweight Redwood proxy inside our VPC that validates client certs.

We can schedule a technical working session Tuesday afternoon to walk through CSR exchange and the proxy config.

Regards,
Elena Torres
Director, Information Security
Acme Corp
security@acme.com

Elena — thanks, that is very clear and actionable.

Summary & next steps (owners):
- Trust model: Acme will provide a signed intermediate and keep keys in their HSM. (Owner: Acme PKI)
- CSR workflow: Redwood infra (Karthik & Jonas) to draft CSR exchange and automated rotation proposal. We'll include ACME-compatible and CSR-pull options. (Owner: Karthik, due 2025-03-07)
- Split DNS: Acme to own private zones and expose resolver peering; Redwood to configure resolver chaining and optional shadow zone as fallback. (Owner: Acme platform / Grace to coordinate)
- mTLS proxy: Redwood infra to prepare a reference lightweight proxy (Envoy) that runs in Acme VPC and enforces mutual TLS both inbound/outbound as requested. (Owner: Jonas, prototype due 2025-03-10)
- OCSP stapling verification: Redwood to add a smoke test during deploy and provide stapling logs for week 1. (Owner: Karthik)

I'll schedule a 60-minute working session for Tuesday 2025-03-04 14:00 PT and include a short agenda: CSR handshake, HSM integration notes, Envoy config sketch, and verification checklist.

Attachments: acme-pki-requirements.pdf (from Acme), cert-provenance-matrix.csv (redwood)
